options.label: Keep the earlier /editorial/ edition live but excluded from search, and index only the root site (current).
options.tradeoff: Nothing is lost and there is one indexed site; the old edition is still public if someone has the URL.

options.label: Retire /editorial/ entirely and redirect its URLs to the equivalent root pages.
options.tradeoff: Cleanest signal for search engines; a redirect map has to be written and tested first.

options.label: Merge the better parts of the old edition into the root site and remove the duplicate pages.
options.tradeoff: Best content outcome, most work, and the old edition's data conflicts with the root data and must be reconciled.

suggestions.recommendation: B once the redirect map is written. Two editions of a five-page site is more surface than the content justifies.

suggestions.topic: Buy buttons while links are untested

options.label: Keep the buy buttons, labelled as provisional and pending a tracking check (current).
options.tradeoff: The site can earn from day one, but an untested link that silently fails credits nothing.

options.label: Hide every buy button until gate G-02 passes.
options.tradeoff: Maximum compliance confidence; the site earns nothing until the owner tests.

suggestions.recommendation: A, but test within the first week. A page that cannot be clicked is a brochure.

options.label: Run tools/collector.mjs on a small VPS the owner controls, behind HTTPS.
options.tradeoff: Full control of raw data; the owner runs a server and patches it.

options.label: Run it as a serverless function on a platform that supports Node.
options.tradeoff: No server to patch; cold starts and platform limits on storage.

options.label: Skip self-hosting and use a privacy-focused hosted analytics service.
options.tradeoff: Fastest to start; one more third party, and the data leaves your control.

options.label: Stay inactive until there is traffic worth measuring (current).
options.tradeoff: Zero maintenance; decisions stay on instinct, which is exactly what the brief asks to avoid.

suggestions.recommendation: B. It removes the server maintenance objection without handing the data away.

options.label: Show no prices; every button reads 'Check the current price on Amazon' (current).
options.tradeoff: Always accurate, and compliant with the price clause; readers have to click to know a budget.

options.label: Enroll in the Creators API and display Amazon-served prices with a timestamp.
options.tradeoff: Better for budget-led shoppers; more engineering, and a stale price is a compliance risk.

options.label: Show a coarse price band instead of a figure.
options.tradeoff: Useful and stable; still a claim that needs checking, and it ages badly.

suggestions.recommendation: A until traffic justifies the Creators API work. Then B.

options.label: One new guide every two weeks (current).
options.tradeoff: Sustainable; slow to build a topic cluster.

options.label: One new guide per week.
options.tradeoff: Faster topical coverage; needs a real writing slot weekly.

options.label: A batch of eight guides before launch, then monthly.
options.tradeoff: Reaches a useful site size quickly; risks thin pages if the batch is rushed.

suggestions.recommendation: A, at a quality bar high enough that every guide earns its place. Ten thin guides are worse than four good ones.

options.label: No email capture yet; the RSS feed is the only subscription route (current).
options.tradeoff: Nothing to maintain and no consent obligations; no direct channel to readers.

options.label: Add a single-field email capture with double opt-in on guide pages.
options.tradeoff: Owns the audience instead of renting it from search; adds a privacy notice and a provider.

options.label: Publish a 'notify me when a new guide ships' link that opens a mail draft.
options.tradeoff: Zero infrastructure and honest; very low conversion.

suggestions.recommendation: B, and the precondition it named is now met: ten guides are published, so there is something to return for. What is still missing is the provider and a consent route, both of which need an account you own - which is why this stays a choice and not a build. Until then the RSS feed is the only subscription path, and it is linked in the footer of every page.

options.label: Keep editorial illustration, clearly labelled as not the reviewed unit (current).
options.tradeoff: Consistent look, no licensing exposure, no misleading product photography.

options.label: Use Amazon-hosted product images through the approved image service.
options.tradeoff: Shows the actual product; images must be served by Amazon's tools and can change without notice.

options.label: Commission real photography of the units.
options.tradeoff: Highest trust and highest cost; needs physical units.

suggestions.recommendation: B for the product hero on each product page, A everywhere else. Readers want to see the actual thing they are buying.

options.label: Keep the team byline, flagged as a weakness (current).
options.tradeoff: Honest and unchanging; weaker trust signal than a person.

options.label: Add a named editor with a short bio and a contact address.
options.tradeoff: Strongest trust signal; a person has to be accountable for the corrections.

suggestions.recommendation: B as soon as a real person will take the byline. This is one of the cheapest trust wins available.

options.label: Stay at five submitted products and go deep on them (current).
options.tradeoff: Focused and honest; a thin catalogue for a shopping site.

options.label: Add three to five comparison products per category, researched the same way.
options.tradeoff: Makes the categories credible; each added product needs its own source page and verification.

options.label: Expand into a second niche once the first converts.
options.tradeoff: Scales the model; splits attention before anything is proven.

suggestions.recommendation: B, one category at a time, and only where a manufacturer page exists to verify against.

options.label: Dark disclosure bar directly under the masthead, repeated in the footer (current).
options.tradeoff: Impossible to miss, and slightly heavy visually.

options.label: A lighter inline notice above the first product, plus the footer repeat.
options.tradeoff: Prettier; risks being read as decoration rather than disclosure.

suggestions.recommendation: A. The FTC standard is that the disclosure must be hard to miss, and this one is.

options.label: Index the root publication only; keep the other editions reachable but excluded from search, and list them on one archive page (current).
options.tradeoff: One site to rank, no content deleted, and each other edition keeps its own generator and gate if the owner later wants it on its own domain.

options.label: Publish the other editions on separate domains, each with its own tracking ID.
options.tradeoff: Cleanest separation, but it needs three domains, three Associates declarations and three link sets to maintain.

options.label: Unpublish the other editions and keep only their pages in the repository history.
options.tradeoff: The strongest single signal, and the least reversible: the URLs stop resolving and the archived editions become invisible to readers who had them.

suggestions.recommendation: A for now. One indexed site is what the brief asks for, nothing is deleted, and option B stays open because each edition is already a self-contained build.

options.label: Publish the buy button against the observed listing ASIN, with the model-correspondence caveat written on the product page (current).
options.tradeoff: The reader gets a working, tagged link to the exact unit the submitted link resolves to, and the honest caveat is one click away.

options.label: Keep the button hidden until the listing model field confirms the F1 Ace.
options.tradeoff: The tightest possible claim, at the cost of one of five products having no way to buy, which reads to a buyer as broken.

options.label: Point the button at the manufacturer F1 Ace page instead of the Amazon listing.
options.tradeoff: Breaks the affiliate link and the tracking the site exists for.

suggestions.recommendation: A. The product identity is confirmed by two independent observations and the feature match is exact; what is unconfirmed is a model name, which is a labelling question, not an identity question.

options.label: Publish /compare/: one table of the five products on published specifications only, with a blank cell wherever a maker is silent (current).
options.tradeoff: It is the page a buyer actually wants and the strongest internal link target for every guide.

options.label: Keep the comparison inside the shop table and the category pages only.
options.tradeoff: Fewer pages to maintain, and buyers must assemble the comparison themselves from a twelve-column table.

options.label: Add comparison products beyond the five submitted rows so the table has more than one option per category.
options.tradeoff: More useful to a buyer, but each added product needs the same verification work and none of them has been submitted by the owner.

suggestions.recommendation: A now, and C later if Q-01 and Q-02 are closed and there is budget for real product research.

suggestions.topic: Derive every count on a page from the rows that page counts
suggestions.problem: This repository has shipped the same class of bug four times: a shop page saying 'four short links resolved' above a table of five; a resolved flag rendered as open; a source row naming three ASINs after the data said five; an empty category page under a heading that promised an explanation. Each time a sentence was written once by hand and never re-derived from the data it described. Two knowns in the questions register were superseded the same way and are now marked rather than deleted.

options.label: Fix each instance when it is found, which is what has happened so far.
options.tradeoff: Works until the next one. Nothing prevents recurrence, and the instances have been found by later sessions rather than by the build.

options.label: Add a gate rule banning hand-written count phrases in templates, and require the computed form instead.
options.tradeoff: A few hours. Catches the class rather than the instance.

options.label: Add a build assertion that no rendered section has a non-empty heading over an empty body, and that every collection rendered on a page is non-empty unless the page says so.
options.tradeoff: Cheaper than B and it also catches the empty-page case.

suggestions.recommendation: B and C together. They are the only rows on this page that prevent a defect rather than describe one, and both are small. CI now catches a stale generated file, which is adjacent but different: it cannot see a sentence that was wrong the first time it was written.

suggestions.topic: Record the two policy clauses that constrain the AI half of the brief
suggestions.problem: The brief asks for an AI-powered platform that automates product research and pricing analysis. Two clauses read verbatim in this session's re-fetch bear on that directly and neither had been recorded: §5 bars using Special Links or Program Content to develop machine learning models without Amazon's express prior written approval, and §6(y) bars price tracking or alerting functionality on the Site unless Amazon agrees.

options.label: Treat the automation in the brief as unqualified and build it.
options.tradeoff: The fastest path to what the brief describes and the likeliest path to a material breach, which permits immediate termination under Operating Agreement §6.

options.label: Build only automation that touches no Special Link and no Program Content: internal registers, the build, the gate, the analytics pipeline, and drafts written from manufacturer pages with citations. Keep pricing analysis off the Site. Ask Amazon about §5 before going further.
options.tradeoff: Slower, and part of the brief stays unbuilt. Everything already in this repository is inside it.

options.label: Request PA API / Creators API access and Amazon's written approval, then build the full pipeline.
options.tradeoff: The only route to prices, ratings and the automated research the brief describes. Needs an approved account and a qualifying site, so it depends on S-02 and Q-03.

suggestions.recommendation: B now and C as the destination. Published on the compliance page in this session so the boundary is visible to whoever builds next rather than rediscovered later.

suggestions.topic: A privacy notice for the click counter
suggestions.problem: Participation Requirements §3(e) requires disclosing cookies, pixels and other technologies and how visitor data is collected, used, stored and disclosed. The site loads a click counter on every page and, until this session, published no notice anywhere on the live surface. Privacy pages existed only under legacy/, belonging to superseded editions.

options.label: Ship no notice.
options.tradeoff: The counter sets no cookies and the endpoint is empty, so nothing is presently collected. The obligation to disclose the technology does not obviously disappear because the endpoint is unset.

options.label: Publish a short /privacy/ page stating what the counter does, what it does not collect, that the endpoint is unset, and what would change if a third-party analytics product were adopted.
options.tradeoff: An hour, and done in this session for review. It is a draft of a legal-adjacent page and should be read rather than trusted.

options.label: Adopt a hosted consent and privacy service.
options.tradeoff: Proportionate for a site with a real audience and third-party processors. Overkill now, and it adds a processor of its own.

suggestions.recommendation: B, implemented in this session as a draft. It closes Q-11 and answers part of Q-16; whether the wording is adequate where the site is operated from is a question for counsel, not something a build session should settle.

suggestions.problem: Two product registers are maintained: data/products.json for the root site and data/register/products.json for /editorial/. They disagreed once, in a way that attributed a meat thermometer to the wrong submitted link, and the disagreement was caught only because a later session re-read both. Every verified fact is currently held twice.

options.label: Keep both and re-check them against each other each session (current).
options.tradeoff: No migration risk. The check is manual, and manual checks here have a documented record of being missed.

options.label: Add a gate rule that fails the build when the two registers disagree on any shared field for any product.
options.tradeoff: About an hour. It does not remove the duplication but it makes disagreement impossible to ship, which is the failure that actually happened.

options.label: Merge into one register with per-publication views.
options.tradeoff: Removes the duplication permanently. The largest data change available here, and it touches files two earlier sessions built.

suggestions.recommendation: B now, and C if S-01 chooses to consolidate the publications. B is a few dozen lines and converts a class of silent error into a build failure.

suggestions.topic: Should the gate tell a product link apart from a citation?
suggestions.problem: The root gate marks every amazon.com anchor rel="sponsored". For the links that pay for this site that is exactly what Google's guidance asks for. For a citation to Amazon's own help or privacy pages it is a misstatement, because Google reserves sponsored for advertisements and paid placements and says a regular link needs no rel at all. The editorial publication reached the opposite answer and marks its citations class="cite" rel="nofollow", enforced by its own gate. Both are defensible; they are not the same policy, and this session hit the difference while writing /privacy/.

options.label: Keep the blanket rule and cite Amazon help pages as plain text rather than linking them (what /privacy/ does now).
options.tradeoff: Impossible to ship an unmarked product link, which is the failure that matters. It costs a few convenience links, and a plain-text URL is worse on a phone.

options.label: Make the rule precise and fail-closed: a link is product-intent if it targets /dp/, carries tag= or carries data-outbound, and must then be both sponsored and tagged; any other amazon.com link must not be sponsored. Anything that cannot be classified fails the build.
options.tradeoff: Semantically correct against Google's guidance and it restores citation links. It is a change to a compliance gate, so it needs a negative test written first and should not be made by a build session on its own authority.

options.label: Keep the blanket rule for product links and allow a short explicit allowlist of informational Amazon paths, checked literally.
options.tradeoff: Narrower than B and easier to audit, because the allowlist is short and visible. It grows by hand and someone will eventually add a path they should not have.

suggestions.recommendation: B, with the negative test written first: break a product link's tag, confirm the build fails, then make the change. Do not adopt B without that test, because the blanket rule is currently one of the things standing between this site and an untagged outbound link.

suggestions.topic: A house style rule that can be checked
suggestions.problem: 'Do not read like AI slop' is not implementable as stated, and every attempt to implement a vague instruction produces vague output. It becomes implementable as a short list of forbidden patterns a build can test, plus a page of concrete before-and-after examples drawn from this site's own copy.

options.label: Rely on editorial judgement per page.
options.tradeoff: Free, and it is how the current copy was produced - which is good enough that the diagnosis is worth writing down rather than repeating.

options.label: Publish a house style file with do/don't rules and real before-and-after examples from this site, and check the mechanical parts in the gate: banned opener phrases, headings that are not claims, uniform list-item length within a section.
options.tradeoff: Half a day. The gate catches the mechanical failures; the rest stays editorial. Publishing the standard does more for reader trust than any badge.

options.label: Add a readability-score threshold per page to the gate.
options.tradeoff: Objective and easy to implement, and it optimises for the wrong thing: it pushes copy toward short dumb sentences, which is its own kind of slop.

suggestions.recommendation: B. The forbidden list and the twelve prescriptions are already written at /design-brief/; what is missing is the gate rule and the decision to hold future copy to it.

suggestions.topic: De-indexing the superseded editions, by the method that actually works
suggestions.problem: Five reader-facing editions of the same five products are published under one host. The root site claimed the others were kept out of the index by robots.txt; Google states that robots.txt 'is not a mechanism for keeping a web page out of Google' (S24) and that 'specifying the noindex rule in the robots.txt file is not supported' (S25). Checking the shipped files, only /editorial/ carries a noindex tag; /counter/, /counterwise/ and /crisp-index/ do not, and the first two advertise sitemaps of their own.

options.label: Add <meta name="robots" content="noindex,follow"> to each secondary edition's own generator, and remove its Disallow line so Googlebot can reach the tag.
options.tradeoff: The correct mechanism per S25, and nothing is deleted. Effort is per edition, and each edition is generated by its own tool, so the change belongs to those files.

options.label: Move every secondary edition under /legacy/ in one commit, so there is exactly one live tree at the root.
options.tradeoff: One indexed publication by construction rather than by instruction. The editions' own generators then point at paths that no longer exist, so each generator has to be told or retired.

options.label: Publish the editions you actually like on their own hosts and leave nothing but /legacy/ here.
options.tradeoff: Best long-term: one topic per domain, no cannibalisation. Costs a domain and a deploy per edition.

options.label: Leave as shipped: secondary editions disallowed for crawling in the root robots.txt, with the over-claim on /flagged/ corrected (this session's change).
options.tradeoff: Removes the false statement and saves crawl budget. It does not de-index anything: a Disallowed URL can still appear in results without a description (S24).

suggestions.recommendation: A for anything you intend to keep on this host, B for anything you do not. D is shipped, and it is the weakest of the four: it is crawl management wearing an indexing decision's clothes.

suggestions.problem: A guide that buries its answer under four headings is a guide a reader leaves, and a page a reader leaves is a page a search engine discounts. The brief's 'not AI slop' instruction is answered by giving the answer plainly, with its sources, before the argument.

options.label: Leave the deck as the only above-the-fold summary.
options.tradeoff: The deck is a teaser by design, so the answer arrives later. Nothing to maintain.

options.label: Add a 'summary' field per guide, rendered as a boxed short answer under the byline, and compute the word and minute count from the guide's own text at build time.
options.tradeoff: Each guide needs a short, honest answer written for it - which also catches a guide that has no answer to give. Implemented for all ten guides in this session; the reading figure is a word count, not a reader measurement.

suggestions.recommendation: B, shipped. If a guide cannot be summarised in four sentences, that is a signal about the guide, not the format.

suggestions.topic: How much structured data to publish
suggestions.problem: The site emits Article on guides and Product on product pages. Question-shaped guides with questions and answers on the page, and a three-level hierarchy under one root, are both describable in machine-readable form, which is the cheapest findability lever that needs no owner action.

options.label: Article only (as shipped before this session).
options.tradeoff: Minimal and valid; nothing about the site structure or the Q&A content is declared.

options.label: An @graph per guide: Article (with wordCount, section, inLanguage) + BreadcrumbList, plus FAQPage where the guide carries questions and answers.
options.tradeoff: Implemented in this session. It buys machine-readable structure, not a rich result: Google shows FAQ rich results mainly for well-known authoritative sites, so this is stated as structure, not as a SERP promise.

options.label: Add Product offers and price data.
options.tradeoff: Not available while the site publishes no prices: the price clause (S03) and the no-republished-prices rule (FLG-016) both stand until the Associates Creators API is enrolled, which is S-04 option B.

suggestions.recommendation: B, shipped, and do not sell it as a rich-result win. C waits for an API enrolment decision.

suggestions.topic: What the buy links should be
suggestions.problem: Every button on the site is a constructed URL of the form amazon.com/dp/<observed ASIN>?tag=<tracking id>. That matches the tag format the Program Policies describe, and it is honest: the ASIN is what the submitted short link was observed landing on. But it is not a Special Link generated in Associates Central, and the submitted short links themselves are not reproducible - in the latest round four of four resolved to the Amazon home page (FLG-031), which is exactly why they are not published as buttons (FLG-003).

options.label: Keep the constructed tagged links (current).
options.tradeoff: Works today and every destination is the observed one. Credits nothing until gate G-02 is passed, and it is a URL this site assembled rather than one Amazon issued.

options.label: Wait: show no buy button until a Special Link exists for each product.
options.tradeoff: Maximum certainty, zero earning, and a shop with no doors.

options.label: Keep A, and paste a generated Special Link into each product row as soon as one exists per product; the register then carries both, dated, and the build prefers the Amazon-issued one.
options.tradeoff: Recommended. One test per product, no downtime, and the link a reader clicks becomes the link Amazon issued rather than the link we assembled.

suggestions.recommendation: C. Until it is done, /how-we-choose/ and the shop table both say the links are constructed and untested, which is the true statement the site is built on.

suggestions.topic: A dated re-check ritual for listing copy
suggestions.problem: Three sessions have re-read the five listings and matched the titles each time; the most recent pass could not fetch amazon.com at all, so it re-derived nothing (FLG-039). Listing titles, included accessories and prices change without notice, and this site publishes the title it saw with a date on it. That is honest, but it quietly ages.

options.label: Leave the dated reads as they are and let the dates speak.
options.tradeoff: Zero work. A reader sees 'observed November 20, 2026' and can judge staleness themselves.

options.label: Add a monthly 10-minute manual re-check, recorded in data/observations/ and shown on each product page as a last-seen date.
options.tradeoff: Recommended, and it is the only check that sees the page a shopper sees. Needs a person, which is why it is a suggestion and not an automation claim.

options.label: Automate the fetch in CI.
options.tradeoff: Rejected on the evidence: unauthenticated fetches of Amazon fail or land on the home page in this environment, so a scheduled job would raise a red flag every week for a reason that means nothing. Do not build an alarm that cannot be trusted.

suggestions.recommendation: B. And explicitly not C - a check that fails for reasons unrelated to the fact it claims to verify is worse than no check, which is the same logic behind gate G-02.

suggestions.topic: A citation-integrity check for the registers
suggestions.problem: Three citation defects were found by hand in this repository in one day: a flag crediting the 10-post rule of thumb to a manufacturer page (FLG-038), a workflow paragraph crediting the publishing cadence to the wrong suggestion (FLG-040), and a stray degree sign inside a feature name that both official pages write plainly (FLG-037). None of them breaks a build. All of them break a reader's trust, and the second one is exactly the kind of error a 'we verified everything' site cannot afford.

options.label: Rely on reviewers noticing.
options.tradeoff: Three were missed for days and found by a session reading text against sources rather than a machine.

options.label: Check every cross-reference in the registers at the gate: every S-id, FLG-id and S-id suggestion token appearing inside any data string must resolve to a real row.
options.tradeoff: Implemented in this session's verify.mjs. It cannot judge whether a sentence is well written; it can make a dangling or wrong-numbered citation fail the build.

options.label: Also require each guide sentence to carry an inline source id.
options.tradeoff: Maximum auditability, and it makes every guide read like a legal filing. The bottom-of-page source list plus the product-page grid already do this job where the facts live.

suggestions.recommendation: B, shipped. Prose stays readable; the wiring is what gets tested.

note: Every item here is a decision waiting on the owner. Nothing is implemented until an option is chosen, except where a row says it was implemented in this session - those were done because leaving them undone meant shipping a known defect, and each is reversible in one commit and is listed here for review. Reply with the suggestion ID and the option letter, for example “S-01 B”. S-11 to S-19 were added by session 66f2548a on 2026-11-20; numbering continues from main's S-10 because this branch had independently used S-11 to S-25 and those rows were dropped rather than renumbered over the top of main's. Four of the dropped rows duplicated topics main already carries: imagery, the byline, reader capture and pricing display. S-20 to S-25 were added by session b7320829-affil3 on 2026-11-20, after a verification round that read seven official pages first-hand and found three citation defects in these registers. S-21, S-22 and S-25 are implemented in that session and listed here for reversal as well as approval; S-20 and S-24 are owner decisions with the exact mechanism named; S-23 is the one that changes whether the site earns.

tracks.name: 1. Unblock revenue
tracks.why: Nothing here earns until a tagged Special Link exists and has been tested once against the tracking report. These rows come first and are owner-access work measured in minutes, not build work.

tracks.name: 2. Reader trust and publication polish
tracks.why: The rows that decide whether this reads as something a person published: a byline, pictures, navigation in reader vocabulary, and a house style that can be checked rather than hoped for.

tracks.name: 3. Findability
tracks.why: One publication for a crawler to index, a sitemap and feed that grow with each guide, and a way to see which queries actually arrive. Without the last of those, the next topic is chosen by instinct.

tracks.name: 4. Measurement
tracks.why: Click and conversion counting, the ledger, and reader capture. Deliberately after findability: measuring a page nobody can find produces zeros, and zeros are not a signal.

tracks.name: 5. Compliance gates
tracks.why: Rules enforced by the build rather than remembered by an editor. Three clauses read verbatim in this session's re-fetch had never been recorded, and two of them change what may be built at all.

tracks.name: 6. Platform and repo machinery
tracks.why: Registers, gates and the failure modes that produced real errors in this repository's own history. Cheap to fix, and they are what stops the same mistake recurring.

how_to_use: Read the tracks in order. Track 1 is owner-access work measured in minutes and it gates everything else: until one tagged link has been tested against a tracking report, the site cannot earn and no amount of design work changes that. Track 2 is the answer to 'it should not read like AI slop' and is deliberately concrete. Tracks 3 and 4 are findability and measurement. Track 5 records clauses found in this session's verbatim re-read that constrain what may be built at all. Track 6 is the machinery, and it is where this repository's own repeated bugs came from.

sequence.why: Gate G-02. One tagged link tested once against the tracking report, before anything scales. Minutes of owner time; unblocks all revenue. §6(u) rules out testing it by purchase.
Decide the automation boundary before building more automation, not after. Two clauses constrain it and neither was recorded until now.
Settle how many publications exist before verifying Search Console, or you submit a sitemap for pages you may then retire. robots.txt already disallows the secondary ones.
A named byline changes every template and every piece of copy, and §2(b) means any credential stated has to be true.
A checkable house style is what stops the next page regressing. The prescriptions already exist at /design-brief/.
Imagery, once the byline and style exist to hang it on.
Navigation labels, after the name and byline, so the words match the publication.
Search Console, after S-01, so the next topic is chosen from measured queries rather than instinct.
An analytics endpoint with an owner. Meaningless before there is traffic to measure, and S-16 should be settled first.
Reader capture, after S-12 and after the privacy notice is reviewed. §4 requires opt-in and §6(g) bars rewarding a click.
Cadence, once S-13 can say what to write next.
Do this first instead if you would rather stop the drift bugs than improve the look. It is the cheapest row here.
